title: Parsing in-memory data is slow
description:
Currently when passing string data to ‘vroom’ (i.e. via `vroom::vroom(I(mydata), ...)`) it writes that memory out to disk into a temporary file before reading the data back in. Unfortunately this round-trip adds a *substantial* overhead: in a quick test, reading a memory-based table with 200k rows (~ 50 MiB) was almost *2.5 times slower* than a disk-based file (1.47s±0.41 *vs.* 0.59±0.06). And it’s slower than using `read.csv()` (including manual data conversion). This is a single data point, though reproducible for the same data.

Interestingly, using shared memory/tmpfs doesn’t help very much: the overhead probably comes mostly from the actual copying of the data and the kernel context switching at the file IO boundary.

This might well be out of scope for ‘vroom’. — If I understand correctly, the whole point of this package is the memory-based indexing/lazy loading of disk storage. However, ‘vroom’ is now the backing implementation for ‘readr’, and it would be great if ‘readr’ efficiently supported memory-based data as a first-class citizen.

(My use-case is tabular data received as CSV from a web API, so the data never needs to hit the disk. The web API in question specifically returns CSV because JSON would be too large/slow. Of course receiving data over the network will usually be slower than disk access anyway, so the actual overhead is a lot less than the 2.5x quoted above.)

title: Error when using numeric reference in col_select and id in read_csv
description:
I have a strange error when I try to use the id argument in read_csv together with the col_select() **but** only if I refer to the columns using their numeric position eg.c(1:3)

Specifically when you import multiple csv files from a file path using readr::read_csv, use the id argument and use the col_select argument by referencing the columns by position in either in total or in a non-continuous way then there is either an error or it will drop a column.

However if we delete the id argument, and use the same numeric reference then it will work.

There are many workarounds to this (eg. referring to the columns by name, etc) however sometimes I'm referring to 100's of columns so using numeric position is very handy. 

Please see below for reproducible example:
``` 
df1 <- data.frame(a=1:10,
                 b=letters[1:10],
                 c=1:10,
                 d=1:10,row.names = F)
  
df2 <- data.frame(a=11:20,
                  b=letters[11:20],
                  c=11:20,
                  d=11:20,row.names = F)


write.csv(x = df1,"df1.csv",row.names = F)
write.csv(x = df2,"df2.csv",row.names=F)

files <- c("df1.csv","df2.csv")

#works, brings in everything
read_csv(files,id = "source")

#works but is missing column "d"
read_csv(files,col_select = 1:4,id="source")

#Does not work, "Error: argument of length 0"; try reference "5th" column but it doesn't exist
read_csv(files,col_select = 1:5,id="source")

#does not work,Error: Can't subset columns that don't exist.                                                                                                                
read_csv(files,col_select =c(1,3:4),id="source")

#however this works, notice the missing id argument
read_csv(files,col_select =c(1,3:4))


```

title: vroom generates large temporary files that are not deleted
description:
I am trying to investigate some large files (20 to 100 million observations) using `vroom_lines` on a Windows computer (a server to which I remote access)

```
library(tidyverse)
library(vroom)

fs <- list.files()
for( f in fs){
   vroom_lines(altrep=T,progress=T) %>% lenght %>% print
}
```

As `vroom_lines` runs the available space in disc `C:` (windows base disk) keeps decreasing quickly until it eats all 36.5Gb of disk space. In the loop above, after `vroom_line` concludes the first iteration of the loop the disk use does not decrease. If I interrupt the R session disk use also is only partially reduced. Finally, only if I sign out of the server the disk space in `C:` is restored. Therefore I am assuming that only by signing out the temporary files are deleted.

UPDATE: I just checked  `tempdir() %>% list.files` after running  `vroom_lines` in a 0.8Gb file. The command leaves behind a 10Gb tempfile after execution has stopped.

UPDATE2: `tempdir %>% list.files(full_paths=T) %>% file.remove` returns an error message saying I don't have permission to remove the file. So part of the problem may be specific to the server user permissons. However such a large temp-file is weird.

Also. the file being read is of fwf  (position delimited) type.

UPDATE3: I initially diagnosed this with `vroom_lines` but the `vroom` function also generates very large temporary files.

The script reads the first four files without a problem but crashes R when it tries to read either of the last two: sm_state, sm_supersector. It does this in RStudio and the R GUI. Inspecting the two files in a text editor doesn't show any special characters.

When I tried to create the reprex, it gave me this message: This reprex appears to crash R. See standard output and standard error for more details.

The standard output and error simply shows that the script correctly downloaded the six files. I've inserted the relevant code below

```r

# packages
```

title: innecesary quotes when string starts with NA

```r
  tibble(col1 = c("JOHN", "NATHAM", "PETER")),
  file = "example.csv"
)
```

produces

```
col1
JOHN
"NATHAM"
PETER
```

but it would be more adequate

```
col1
JOHN
NATHAM
PETER
```

title: `format_csv` segfaults with empty data frame
description:
Hi readr team,

I noticed that passing a data.frame with 0 rows/cols causes a segfault. I think it would be nice to check for this, perhaps in `format_delim` right after the call to check that `is.data.frame(x)` and return an empty string in that case, since in some cases (like mine) I'm using it programmatically to deal with incoming data and there might be genuine empty records, so downstream processing can take care of the empty csv.

I am using readr version 2.1.2 with R version 4.0.4.

```r
> library(readr)
> readr::format_csv(data.frame())

 *** caught segfault ***
address 0xffffffffffffffff, cause 'memory not mapped'
```

title: Move vroom from r-lib GitHub Organization to tidyverse
description:
Given the nature of the relationship between readr and vroom, the vast majority of readr issues opened today are actually vroom issues.

Having these two packages reside in repos in separate GitHub Orgs means we can't easily transfer readr issues to vroom.

Therefore I am transferring vroom from r-lib to tidyverse.

There are some downsides (e.g. what should we do about the pkgdown site's URL?), but I think it's a net positive overall.

title: Interface in C/C++ for accessing Altstring/Altrep data
description:
For accessing the underlying string data, I believe the only option is `STRING_ELT` or the analogous Rcpp methods. However, that causes materialization, which as you know is costly. 

If there were a way to access the data (e.g. a C-style string `const char *` and the encoding `cetype_t`) I think that would be a good way for users and package developers to fully take advantage of the Altstring implementation in vroom.

title: locking file when saving
Fractional seconds, col_datetime/col_time differences and %AT
description:
# Data for example
I could have likely made easier example data sets, but this is what I was using at the time (they are public and open):

[62163.csv.gz](https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/files/8353807/62163.csv.gz)
[62163_data.csv.gz](https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/files/8353874/62163_data.csv.gz)
[62163_data_separated.csv.gz](https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/files/8353880/62163_data_separated.csv.gz)

# Description of Issue
Fractional seconds are truncated in `col_time` defaults, but not `col_datetime` defaults and the ask may be a warning if fractional seconds are truncated if `col_time(format = "")` is used for `hms`/time objects.

-------------------------------------------------------

# Reprex 
This is the option needed to set to see fractional seconds when printing

``` r
options(digits.secs = 3)
```

Load `hms` so we can see things as times versus `difftime` objects

``` r
library(hms)
```

# Example with Fractional Seconds

``` r
url = "https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/files/8353807/62163.csv.gz"
file = file.path(tempdir(), basename(url))
if (!file.exists(file)) {
  curl::curl_download(url, file)
}
```

## Data Header

We see the fractional seconds in this file, which is needed for our analysis.

``` r
readLines(file, 5)
#> [1] "DAY_OF_DATA,START_TIME,END_TIME,DATA_QUALITY_FLAG_CODE,DATA_QUALITY_FLAG_VALUE"
#> [2] "2,14:11:35.463000,14:11:35.463000,COUNT_SPIKES_Z,1"                            
#> [3] "2,14:10:00.000000,14:10:59.988000,ADJACENT_INVALID,1"                          
#> [4] "2,14:12:00.000000,14:12:59.988000,ADJACENT_INVALID,1"                          
#> [5] "4,11:17:25.938000,11:17:25.938000,COUNT_SPIKES_Z,1"
```

## Reading data with `vroom`

Here we read the data and see that the output is a `col_time` object

``` r
data = vroom::vroom(file, progress = FALSE)
#> Rows: 15 Columns: 5
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr  (1): DATA_QUALITY_FLAG_CODE
#> dbl  (2): DAY_OF_DATA, DATA_QUALITY_FLAG_VALUE
#> time (2): START_TIME, END_TIME
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
vroom::spec(data)
#> cols(
#>   DAY_OF_DATA = col_double(),
#>   START_TIME = col_time(format = ""),
#>   END_TIME = col_time(format = ""),
#>   DATA_QUALITY_FLAG_CODE = col_character(),
#>   DATA_QUALITY_FLAG_VALUE = col_double(),
#>   .delim = ","
#> )
```

No fractional seconds are printed:

``` r
head(data)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   DAY_OF_DATA START_TIME END_TIME DATA_QUALITY_FLAG_CODE DATA_QUALITY_FLAG_VALUE
#>         <dbl> <time>     <time>   <chr>                                    <dbl>
#> 1           2 14:11:35   14:11:35 COUNT_SPIKES_Z                               1
#> 2           2 14:10:00   14:10:59 ADJACENT_INVALID                             1
#> 3           2 14:12:00   14:12:59 ADJACENT_INVALID                             1
#> 4           4 11:17:25   11:17:25 COUNT_SPIKES_Z                               1
#> 5           4 11:35:21   11:35:21 COUNT_SPIKES_X                               1
#> 6           4 11:16:00   11:16:59 ADJACENT_INVALID                             1
```

We can confirm that they are truncated.

``` r
as.numeric(lubridate::seconds(data$START_TIME[1:5])) %% 1
#> [1] 0 0 0 0 0
as.numeric(data$START_TIME[1:5]) %% 1
#> [1] 0 0 0 0 0
```

## Different `col_time` format

The default `%AT` I don’t think takes into account fractional seconds, so we need to pass our own format in.
Here we specify the `col_time` so that it uses `%OS`, which I think is R-specific as per `?strptime`

``` r
col_time_with_frac_secs = function(...) {
  vroom::col_time(format = "%H:%M:%OS", ...)
}
```

read in the data

``` r
data = vroom::vroom(file,
                   col_types =
                     vroom::cols(
                       START_TIME = col_time_with_frac_secs(),
                       END_TIME = col_time_with_frac_secs(),
                     ))
```

Fractional seconds are preserved

``` r
as.numeric(lubridate::seconds(data$START_TIME[1:5])) %% 1
#> [1] 0.463 0.000 0.000 0.938 0.800
as.numeric(data$START_TIME[1:5]) %% 1
#> [1] 0.463 0.000 0.000 0.938 0.800
```
------------------------------------

# Discussion of Issue/Resolution
Overall, that may be the end of it to be an issue to point to people in the future. I’m not sure if there should be warning that things may be truncated or whether this should/could guess fractional seconds. Below I just show that the default for a `datetime` does preserve fractional seconds, so this behavior is mildly inconsistent, and the format of how you store dates and times can lead to fractional second differences.

------------------------------------
# Example File with Datetime versus time object
If we have a file with a `datetime`, then this doesn’t seem to be an issue:


``` r
url = "https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/files/8353874/62163_data.csv.gz"
file = file.path(tempdir(), basename(url))
if (!file.exists(file)) {
  curl::curl_download(url, file)
}
```

## Data Header

We see the fractional seconds in this file.

``` r
readLines(file, 5)
#> [1] "HEADER_TIMESTAMP,X,Y,Z"                    
#> [2] "2000-01-08 17:30:00.000,0.208,0.079,-0.751"
#> [3] "2000-01-08 17:30:00.013,0.17,0.094,-0.751" 
#> [4] "2000-01-08 17:30:00.025,0.22,0.109,-0.727" 
#> [5] "2000-01-08 17:30:00.038,0.258,0.047,-0.78"
```

## Reading data with `vroom`

Here we read the data and see that the output is a `col_datetime` object

``` r
data = vroom::vroom(file, progress = FALSE)
#> Rows: 9 Columns: 4
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> dbl  (3): X, Y, Z
#> dttm (1): HEADER_TIMESTAMP
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
vroom::spec(data)
#> cols(
#>   HEADER_TIMESTAMP = col_datetime(format = ""),
#>   X = col_double(),
#>   Y = col_double(),
#>   Z = col_double(),
#>   .delim = ","
#> )
```

We see fractional seconds are preserved:

``` r
head(data)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   HEADER_TIMESTAMP            X     Y      Z
#>   <dttm>                  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 2000-01-08 17:30:00.000 0.208 0.079 -0.751
#> 2 2000-01-08 17:30:00.013 0.17  0.094 -0.751
#> 3 2000-01-08 17:30:00.024 0.22  0.109 -0.727
#> 4 2000-01-08 17:30:00.037 0.258 0.047 -0.78 
#> 5 2000-01-08 17:30:00.049 0.276 0.029 -0.762
#> 6 2000-01-08 17:30:00.062 0.258 0.032 -0.777
```

We can confirm that they are preserved

``` r
as.numeric(lubridate::seconds(data$HEADER_TIMESTAMP[1:5])) %% 1
#> [1] 0.00000000 0.01300001 0.02499998 0.03799999 0.04999995
as.numeric(data$HEADER_TIMESTAMP[1:5]) %% 1
#> [1] 0.00000000 0.01300001 0.02499998 0.03799999 0.04999995
```

# Example with separated Date and Time - similar issue

If we have a file with 2 columns, separated in date and time, where time has fractional seconds, then this is again an issue as the first example.

``` r
url = "https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/files/8353880/62163_data_separated.csv.gz"
file = file.path(tempdir(), basename(url))
if (!file.exists(file)) {
  curl::curl_download(url, file)
}
```

## Data Header

We see the fractional seconds in this file.

``` r
readLines(file, 5)
#> [1] "DATE,TIMESTAMP,X,Y,Z"                      
#> [2] "2000-01-08,17:30:00.000,0.208,0.079,-0.751"
#> [3] "2000-01-08,17:30:00.013,0.17,0.094,-0.751" 
#> [4] "2000-01-08,17:30:00.025,0.22,0.109,-0.727" 
#> [5] "2000-01-08,17:30:00.038,0.258,0.047,-0.78"
```

## Reading data with `vroom`

Here we read the data and see that the output is a `col_time` object

``` r
data = vroom::vroom(file, progress = FALSE)
#> Rows: 9 Columns: 5
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> dbl  (3): X, Y, Z
#> date (1): DATE
#> time (1): TIMESTAMP
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
vroom::spec(data)
#> cols(
#>   DATE = col_date(format = ""),
#>   TIMESTAMP = col_time(format = ""),
#>   X = col_double(),
#>   Y = col_double(),
#>   Z = col_double(),
#>   .delim = ","
#> )
```

No fractional seconds are printed:

``` r
head(data)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   DATE       TIMESTAMP     X     Y      Z
#>   <date>     <time>    <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 2000-01-08 17:30     0.208 0.079 -0.751
#> 2 2000-01-08 17:30     0.17  0.094 -0.751
#> 3 2000-01-08 17:30     0.22  0.109 -0.727
#> 4 2000-01-08 17:30     0.258 0.047 -0.78 
#> 5 2000-01-08 17:30     0.276 0.029 -0.762
#> 6 2000-01-08 17:30     0.258 0.032 -0.777
```

We can confirm that they are truncated.

``` r
as.numeric(lubridate::seconds(data$TIMESTAMP[1:5])) %% 1
#> [1] 0 0 0 0 0
as.numeric(data$TIMESTAMP[1:5]) %% 1
#> [1] 0 0 0 0 0
```

title: Create multiple columns of the same type
description:
It would be great to make it easier to define multiple columns of the same type to avoid repetition. For example something along the line

```r
    library(vroom)

    fct_cols <- c("success", "attempts")
    yr_cols <- c("birthyr", "firstyr")
    mdy_cols <- c("birthdy")
    chr_cols <- c("name")

    cols_of <- function(col_format, names) {
      col_spec <- rep_len(list(col_format), length.out = length(names))
      setNames(col_spec, names)
    }

    col_spec_list <- c(
      cols_of(col_character(), chr_cols),
      cols_of(col_factor(), fct_cols),
      cols_of(col_date(format = "%Y"), yr_cols),
      cols_of(col_date(format = "%m/%d/%Y"), mdy_cols)
    )
    cols_only(!!!col_spec_list)
    #> cols_only(
    #>   name = col_character(),
    #>   success = col_factor(levels = NULL, ordered = FALSE, include_na = FALSE),
    #>   attempts = col_factor(levels = NULL, ordered = FALSE, include_na = FALSE),
    #>   birthyr = col_date(format = "%Y"),
    #>   firstyr = col_date(format = "%Y"),
    #>   birthdy = col_date(format = "%m/%d/%Y")
    #> )

<sup>Created on 2020-10-26 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>
```

It is already quite easy to do but it would be great to export a function for this or at least document it. If you like the idea I'm happy to add a PR (and one might also want to add that to `readr`).

PS: I discovered an issue for using the `tidyselect` helpers: https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/237 which would also be very nice to have. Unfortunately, it doesn't seem like it is currently worked on. Is this still something on the roadmap?

title: 24 hour date time issue
description:
Date times with 24 in the hour column don't read properly in vroom.

However, the conversion can be made using lubridate::ymd_hm or lubridate::ymd_hms.

``` r
library(vroom)
vroom("date\n2015-06-14 24:00\n2015-06-14 08:01:01", delim=",")
#> Rows: 2
#> Columns: 1
#> Delimiter: ","
#> dttm [1]: date
#> 
#> Use `spec()` to retrieve the guessed column specification
#> Pass a specification to the `col_types` argument to quiet this message
#> # A tibble: 2 x 1
#>   date               
#>   <dttm>             
#> 1 NA                 
#> 2 2015-06-14 08:01:01

# COULD READ AS STRING AND USE lubridate::ymd_hm TO READ
library(lubridate)
#> Warning: package 'lubridate' was built under R version 3.6.3
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'lubridate'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date, intersect, setdiff, union
ymd_hm("2015-06-14 24:00")
#> [1] "2015-06-15 UTC"

# NEED TO USE ymd_hms() IF THERE ARE SECONDS
ymd_hms("2015-06-14 24:01:22")
#> [1] "2015-06-15 00:01:22 UTC"
```

<sup>Created on 2020-07-02 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


Can a similar adaptation be made in vroom?

title: Consider alternative index approaches
description:
When dealing with very large numeric only files the index takes up ~ the same amount of memory as the actual data. 

- We could investigate writing the index to disk and them mmaping that, which would dramatically reduce the memory requirements.
- We could keep the index in memory but compress it with something like lz4 and uncompress it as needed, provided we store some bookkeeping information on what row numbers the blocks correspond to.
- We could do both the above, write the index to disk and uncompress on demand.

title: Automatically recycle col_types argument when it is just a single character
description:
Hello,

I think it would be nice to allow the `col_types` argument to be recycled when it is a single character.

For example, in the current methodology:


``` r
library(readr)

# only the first column is read as character
read_csv(I("x,y\n1,2\n3,4"), col_types = "c")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   x         y
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 1         2
#> 2 3         4

# have to manually write cc for both
read_csv(I("x,y\n1,2\n3,4"), col_types = "cc")
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   x     y    
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 1     2    
#> 2 3     4

# or specify a cols spec
read_csv(I("x,y\n1,2\n3,4"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   x     y    
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 1     2    
#> 2 3     4
```

<sup>Created on 2022-02-22 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

I think it would be much more convenient if the `col_types` argument was recycled in the same way as for e.g. `googlesheets4::read_sheet`:

``` r
library(googlesheets4)
read_sheet(
    gs4_example("mini-gap"),
    sheet = "Europe",
    range = "A:D",
    col_types = "c"
)

#> v Reading from "mini-gap".
#> v Range ''Europe'!A:D'.
#> # A tibble: 5 x 4
#>   country                continent year  lifeExp
#>   <chr>                  <chr>     <chr> <chr>  
#> 1 Albania                Europe    1952  55.23  
#> 2 Austria                Europe    1952  66.8   
#> 3 Belgium                Europe    1952  68     
#> 4 Bosnia and Herzegovina Europe    1952  53.82  
#> 5 Bulgaria               Europe    1952  59.6
```

title: Add rowname option
description:
Thanks for thisgreat package!

Similar to https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/issues/222 that has been closed. 

Although tidy data do not have row names, not all data in the wild are tidy. The suggested `tibble::column_to_rownames` is not sufficient because when reading a table whose first column is row name, the last column will be dropped, and the first column's name will be used as the rowname's column name, second column's name will be used as the first column name, so on and so forth.

title: Extraneous whitespace complicates parsing in the presence of quoted fields
description:
Based on issues originally reported in readr:
https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/1237
https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/1350

readr 1e tolerates gratuitous whitespace when parsing quoted fields, which can be nice for human readability. But readr 2e, i.e. vroom, does not. Do we want to do anything about that?

``` r
library(readr)
library(vroom)

with_edition(1,
  read_csv('
     "X1",  "X2"
    "a,b", "c,d"',
  show_col_types = FALSE
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   X1    X2   
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 a,b   c,d

with_edition(2,
  read_csv('
     "X1",  "X2"
    "a,b", "c,d"',
  show_col_types = FALSE
  )
)
#> Warning: One or more parsing issues, see `problems()` for details
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   X1    X2            
#>   <chr> <chr>         
#> 1 a     "b\", \"c,d\""

vroom(I('
   "X1",  "X2"
  "a,b", "c,d"'),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
#> Warning: One or more parsing issues, see `problems()` for details
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   X1    X2            
#>   <chr> <chr>         
#> 1 a     "b\", \"c,d\""
```

title: vroom 1.4.0 does not consider locale in guessing delimiters
description:
I love the delimiter guessing of vroom! But it only works for me with  points as decimal marks!  In Europe we encounter often CSV files with commas as decimal marks!

`vroom("0,0;3,0\n1,3;5,8",locale = locale(decimal_mark=","),col_names=FALSE)`

the unexpected result is:

```
# A tibble: 2 x 3
     X1 X2       X3
  <dbl> <chr> <dbl>
1     0 0;3       0
2     1 3;5       8
```
And if I am trying to enforce the column types:

`vroom("0,0;3,0\n1,3;5,8",locale = locale(decimal_mark=","),col_names=FALSE,col_types="dd")`

it says:

`Error: Unnamed `col_types` must have the same length as `col_names`.`

title: vroom na option being ignored for factors
description:
Hello,
I have an issue using the `na` option in vroom. (I was initially using readr but saw that vroom is being used by readr).

```
test.df = data.frame(a=c("missed","a","b"),b=c(1,2,3),c=c(4,5,6))
write.csv(test.df,"test.csv",row.names = FALSE)
x = vroom::vroom("test.csv",na="missed",col_types=cols(a=col_factor(),b=col_integer(),c=col_integer()))
summary(x)
```

I get the following output:
```
      a           b             c      
 missed:1   Min.   :1.0   Min.   :4.0  
 a     :1   1st Qu.:1.5   1st Qu.:4.5  
 b     :1   Median :2.0   Median :5.0  
            Mean   :2.0   Mean   :5.0  
            3rd Qu.:2.5   3rd Qu.:5.5  
            Max.   :3.0   Max.   :6.0
```

My understanding is that 'missed' should have been read as a missing value. Apologies if I'm misunderstanding the option.

title: Possibly don't need to use connections with files that don't end with newlines
description:
If I am reading the POSIX spec correctly it allows you to mmap a file longer than the filename and guarantees the extra bytes until the next page will be zero padded. So you should be able to always mmap the file to file_size + 1 and guarantee it will end with a newline or zero byte.

title: Inconsistency in accepted formats for file argument
description:
Hello,

I was in the progress of updating one of my packages (laboratory results PDF into tibble) that depend on `readr`. During that process I updated the dependency packages and introduced some errors due to different handling in edition/version 2 of `readr`.

Specifically, I was calling `readr::fwf_empty` with a file argument that was a vector of rows from a table I wanted to parse. With the updated dependencies it tries to look for a file in the first position of the vector. So I read the documentation and found that literal data should be one string now. However, by accident I discovered that just adding a newline at the end to each vector element also solved the issue. Let me illustrate with a short example:
```
file <- vroom_example("mtcars-4.csv")
table_lines <- read_lines(file)

# 1. This will error, no file table_lines[1] in current directory
vroom(table_lines)

# 2. Same vector of rows but with \n at the end of each element works
vroom(paste(table_lines, "\n"))

# 3. A single string with line breaks between rows work
vroom(paste(table_lines, collapse = "\n"))
```

Right now I changed to do (2), since in my codebase it was a 1 line change. I have a lot of other functions that sanitizes/verifies my tables based on a vector of rows format. It is quite handy to have `vroom_result[x,]` corresponding to `table_lines[x]`.  But it also means I have a textual `\n` in the last column that I need to clean out.

Simply, I am wondering if the break to using vector of rows (1) is intended. Secondy, if it is coincidence that adding `\n` works, and that I should switch to use a single literal string instead.

Thank you for a wonderful package family.

Best regards  /NFA

title: vroom unhelpful for large data files on /tmp with tmpfs file system
description:
One of the great things about `vroom` is being able to read data out-of-memory and operate on it using native R code. However, this fails when /tmp is mounted as tmpfs, because `vroom` stores temporary files, taking up RAM in these cases, completely negating the out-of-memory advantage.

 I know tmpfs for /tmp is at least the default for Linux distributions such as openSUSE (which I use). So it would be helpful to have an option to choose where temporary files would be stored. Is there such an option?

Edit: I think this is really only an issue with compressed files. Otherwise `vroom` doesn't generate temporary files:
``` r
mygz <- tempfile()
```

title: problems returns incorrect values or throws errors on tables read in other processes
description:
Here is some code that reads a csv file with problems, first in the current R process and then in a child process using both the parallel and future packages:

``` r
library(readr)
library(assertthat)

## Set up a CSV file with problems
problem_file_contents <- "Numeric_Column,Boolean_Column\r\n1,TRUE\r\n2,FALSE\r\n3,NA\r\nBad,Bad"
csv_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write_file(problem_file_contents, csv_file)
## We force specific column types so that some values will cause
## problems
column_spec <- cols(
  Numeric_Column = col_double(),
  Boolean_Column = col_logical()
)

## Read CSV file in-process
x <- read_csv(csv_file, col_types = column_spec)
#> Warning: One or more parsing issues, see `problems()` for details
## We can access the problems just fine
attr(x, "problems")
#> <pointer: 0x7f7f8ed722a0>
print(problems(x))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>     row   col expected           actual file 
#>   <int> <int> <chr>              <chr>  <chr>
#> 1     5     1 a double           Bad    ""   
#> 2     5     2 1/0/T/F/TRUE/FALSE Bad    ""
assert_that(!is.null(attr(x, "problems")))
#> [1] TRUE
assert_that(
  is.data.frame(problems(x)),
  nrow(problems(x)) >= 2
)
#> [1] TRUE

## Try the same thing in a parallel process
library(parallel)
x <- mccollect(mcparallel(read_csv(csv_file, col_types = column_spec)))
## Problems attr is NULL
attr(x, "problems")
#> NULL
## problems table has 0 rows
print(problems(x))
#> # A tibble: 0 × 4
#> # … with 4 variables: row <int>, col <int>, expected <chr>, actual <chr>
assert_that(!is.null(attr(x, "problems")))
#> Error: !is.null(attr(x, "problems")) is not TRUE
assert_that(
  is.data.frame(problems(x)),
  nrow(problems(x)) >= 2
)
#> Error: nrow(problems(x)) not greater than or equal to 2

## Try again, using multicore futures
library(future)
plan(multicore)
## Read a CSV file in a multicore future
x <- value(future(read_csv(csv_file, col_types = column_spec)))
#> Warning: One or more parsing issues, see `problems()` for details
## Pointer points to "0x0", which doesn't look valid
attr(x, "problems")
#> <pointer: 0x0>
## problems throws a bad_weak_ptr error
print(problems(x))
#> Error: bad_weak_ptr

## Try again, using sequential futures
plan(sequential)
## Read a CSV file in a multicore future
x <- value(future(read_csv(csv_file, col_types = column_spec)))
#> Warning: One or more parsing issues, see `problems()` for details
## Pointer looks real
attr(x, "problems")
#> <pointer: 0x7f7f6ef39f20>
## problems returns the expected result
print(problems(x))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>     row   col expected           actual file 
#>   <int> <int> <chr>              <chr>  <chr>
#> 1     5     1 a double           Bad    ""   
#> 2     5     2 1/0/T/F/TRUE/FALSE Bad    ""
assert_that(!is.null(attr(x, "problems")))
#> [1] TRUE
assert_that(
  is.data.frame(problems(x)),
  nrow(problems(x)) >= 2
)
#> [1] TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2021-08-03 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.0)</sup>

As you can see `problems(x)` only works correctly in the first case, when no parallel processes are involved. In the 2nd case, it falsely reports that there were no problems parsing the data, while in the 3rd case, it throws an error. The traceback for this error looks like this:

```
> traceback()
3: vroom_errors_(probs)
2: vroom::problems(x)
1: problems(x)
```

The 4th case shows that the future package itself is not causing issues, since it works with `plan(sequential)`.

Seeing that `class(attr(x, "problems"))` is "externalptr", I assume vroom is generating some kind of pointer that is local to the process it was created with and not accessible after the table is returned to the parent process.

title: R session crashes depending on the size of `guess_max`
description:
Extracted from https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5977

For some reason, the first call to `vroom()` doesn't crash, but the second does (with a larger `guess_max`). I'm not sure why this user is splitting by `\n` since the file uses `;` delimiters, but I think they just wanted it to be read in as a single column of text data that they would post process manually.

I assume the problem is not really with `guess_max`, but somehow vroom is hitting something between lines 101-1000 that it can't handle for some reason.

```r
library(vroom)

url <- "https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/936f6d38-5969-46e5-8b9d-c7646d6390ec"
tf <- tempfile(fileext = ".txt")
download.file(url, tf)

# no crash - even on repeated calls
df <- vroom(
  file = tf, 
  delim = "\n", 
  col_names = FALSE, 
  locale = locale(encoding = "ISO-8859-1")
)

# crashes pretty reliably
df <- vroom(
  file = tf, 
  delim = "\n", 
  col_names = FALSE, 
  locale = locale(encoding = "ISO-8859-1"),
  guess_max = 1000L
)
```

title: Cannot delete files after vroom
description:
I have ran into the issue where I cannot delete files once accessed by `vroom::vroom()` 

This has been discussed in two previous issues (#177 and #280), but these do not seem to resolve the problem as in some cases, the link to the file is still open.

Take this example:
```
write.csv(data.frame(x=1:3,y=c("a","b","c")),"test.csv",row.names=FALSE)
df ​<- vroom::vroom("test.csv")
ps::ps_open_files()
```
This returns a list of the currently opened files (as described in #280). Materializing the object closes this connection
```
vroom:::vroom_materialize(df,FALSE)
ps::ps_open_files()
```
However, this seems to require explicit materialization as merely manipulating the data does not close the connection. Restarting R before the following still shows the connection after `mutate()`:
```
df ​<- vroom::vroom("test.csv")
dplyr::mutate(df,z=paste(x,y))
ps::ps_open_files()
```
It also persists if we delete the object (again restarting R):
```
df <- vroom::vroom("test.csv")
rm(df)
ps::ps_open_files()
```
And it stays if we do not save the object (R restart again to be certain), although figuring out if an object is being stored or not is an entirely different problem:
```
vroom::vroom("test.csv")
ps::ps_open_files()
```

Other than materializing an object (obviously not ideal for large files) or restarting R, how do we close this connection? It would be useful to have a `vroom_delete()` function.

title: Lower performance than expected when doing element-wise indexing
description:
Doing element-wise indexing into vroom's altrep vectors has very high overhead.

``` r
library(vroom)
x <- data.frame(x = runif(1e7))
f <- tempfile()
vroom_write(x, f)

x <- vroom::vroom(f, delim = ",")
#> Rows: 10000000 Columns: 1
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> dbl (1): x
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
my_sum <- function(x) {
sum = 0
for (i in x) {
  if (!is.na(i)) {
    sum = sum + i
  }
}
sum
}
system.time(my_sum(x$x))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>  11.207   0.034  11.258
```

Considerably more than doing the same indexing without altrep.

``` r
library(vroom)
x <- data.frame(x = runif(1e7))
f <- tempfile()
vroom_write(x, f)

x <- vroom::vroom(f, delim = ",", altrep=F)
#> Rows: 10000000 Columns: 1
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> dbl (1): x
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
my_sum <- function(x) {
sum = 0
for (i in x) {
  if (!is.na(i)) {
    sum = sum + i
  }
}
sum
}
system.time(my_sum(x$x))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   1.460   0.006   1.468
```

From profiling this seems to be because we are currently constructing and destructing iterators on every index, e.g. https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/blob/6879455e05a73536e117144b1a6d1a730340bba9/src/vroom_dbl.h#L57

most of the time is spent creating and destroying the objects rather than doing useful work.

Adding another function that calls the `range::at()` member function avoids creating a new iterator each time and mostly rescues the performance.

``` r
library(vroom)
x <- data.frame(x = runif(1e7))
f <- tempfile()
vroom_write(x, f)

x <- vroom::vroom(f, delim = ",")
#> Rows: 10000000 Columns: 1
#> ── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Delimiter: ","
#> dbl (1): x
#> 
#> ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
#> ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.
my_sum <- function(x) {
sum = 0
for (i in x) {
  if (!is.na(i)) {
    sum = sum + i
  }
}
sum
}
system.time(my_sum(x$x))
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   2.855   0.017   2.878
```

title: Double Quotes are interpreted as end-of-string if followed by a delimiter
description:
I have a (python) list that is saved in a csv file using ',' as delimiter and double quotes to escape quotes.
This all works fine until a double quote is followed by a delimiter:

```r
var_1,var_2,var_3
"data", "[""Element1"", ""Element2"", ""Element3""]", "more data"
```
Reading this in I would expect a tibble with three columns.
However, vroom seems to get tripped up and produces this:

```r
  var_1 var_2           var_3
  <chr> <chr>           <chr>
1 data  "[\"Element1\"" "Element2\", \"Element3\"], more data"
```

The second quote after Element1 should be ignored (or the first, as it's the escape character) but it somehow ends the string and interprets the comma as indicating the start of the next value.

Luckily I did not need this list, so I just manually removed the double quotes in bash before reading in the data.
Thanks for all your hard work!

title: na values not respected in numeric columns.
description:
In vroom 1.4.0, the `na` argument to the `vroom()` is not respected for numeric columns if the NA string is numeric. Numeric NA strings are respected in string columns, and non-numeric NA strings are also respected in numeric columns.

For example, if the input file (test2.csv) is as follows:

```
strcol,numcol
foo,1
bar,-9
spam,3
-9,spam
```

and I run `vroom::vroom("test2.csv", na = c("-9", "spam"))`, the output is as follows:

```
# A tibble: 4 x 2
  strcol numcol
  <chr>   <dbl>
1 foo         1
2 bar        -9
3 NA          3
4 NA         NA
```

However, if I use `read_tsv()` from `readr`, the file is properly parsed. The result of `readr::read_csv("test2.csv", na = c("-9", "spam"))` is correct:

```
# A tibble: 4 x 2
  strcol numcol
  <chr>   <dbl>
1 foo         1
2 bar        NA
3 NA          3
4 NA         NA
```

Datasets often use numbers such as -9 or 999 to represent NA in numeric fields, so this is a fairly serious bug, and the inconsistent behavior is also surprising.

title: can't handle embedded nulls in multibyte encoding; need for skipNull argument?
description:
I was trying out `vroom` v 1.4.0.9000 with an 8.8GB tab-delimited text file in UT-16LE encoding (because of  r-lib/vroom@7d54cda ).

`vroom()` returns about half the number of expected rows and some of the character fields contain embedded tabs (the field delimiter!). I can read the same file accurately with `read.delim(skipNull = TRUE)` .

FWIW I am using: Ubuntu 20.10; R 4.1.0; RStudio 1.4.1717

I don't have a reprex: nobody wants an 8.8GB file and encodings are a mystery to me, so I don't know how to dummy up some appropriate data.

Examples:

**- `read.delim(skipNull = TRUE)`**
```
d_rd_skip <- read.delim(
  "data/utf16le.txt", fileEncoding = 'UTF-16LE',
  header = TRUE, sep = "\t", colClasses = "character",
  strip.white = TRUE, na.strings = "",
  skipNul = TRUE,
  quote = "", allowEscapes = FALSE, comment.char = ""
)

dim(d_rd_skip)
#> [1] 9671886      90
# Correct number of rows
# Eyeballing the data frame looks OK
```

**- `read.delim(skipNull = FALSE)`**
```
d_rd_noskip <- read.delim(
  "data/utf16le.txt", fileEncoding = 'UTF-16LE',
  header = TRUE, sep = "\t", colClasses = "character",
  strip.white = TRUE, na.strings = "",
  skipNul = FALSE,
  quote = "", allowEscapes = FALSE, comment.char = ""
)
#> Warning messages:
#> 1: In read.table(file = file, header = header, sep = sep, quote = quote,  :
#>   line 2 appears to contain embedded nulls
#> 2: In read.table(file = file, header = header, sep = sep, quote = quote,  :
#>   line 3 appears to contain embedded nulls
#> 3: In read.table(file = file, header = header, sep = sep, quote = quote,  :
#>   line 4 appears to contain embedded nulls
#> 4: In read.table(file = file, header = header, sep = sep, quote = quote,  :
#>   line 5 appears to contain embedded nulls
#> 5: In scan(file = file, what = what, sep = sep, quote = quote, dec = dec,  :
#>   embedded nul(s) found in input

dim(d_rd_noskip)
#> [1] 9671886      90
# Correct number of rows
# Eyeballing the data frame shows many missing fields from phone_num onwards
```
`read.delim()` complains about embedded nulls, returns the correct number of rows, and some expected field values are missing.
So `skipNull = TRUE` is needed for `read.delim()` to read this file correctly.

**- `vroom()`**
```
library(vroom) # version 1.4.0.9000

d_vr <- vroom(
  "data/utf16le.txt", locale = locale(encoding = "UTF-16LE"),
  col_names = TRUE, delim = "\t", col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
  trim_ws = TRUE, na = "",
  quote = "", escape_double = FALSE, escape_backslash = FALSE, comment = ""
)

dim(d_vr)
#> [1] 4834776      90
# About half the number of rows there should be
# Eyeballing the data frame shows values in the wrong fields and character fields with embedded tabs (the field separator)
```

`vroom()` doesn't give any warnings and hasn't been able to split the characters correctly across the fields.

Many of the arguments to `vroom()` mirror the arguments to `read.delim()`, but there is no equivalent argument in `vroom()` to `skipNull` in `read.delim()`. Perhaps there should be.

Is it possible this issue is related to https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/306 ?

title: Windows Memory Usage Equivalent to Loading Full Dataset
description:
Windows seems to be viewing the memory used by un-materialized ALTREP vectors differently than R. When I load a large CSV file, R reports memory usage as expected (negligible unless columns are materialized); however, Windows task manager reports memory usage roughly equivalent to the full in-memory dataset (see the results at the bottom of the reprex below). This seems to reflect what Windows OS sees; I crashed my machine on a fairly small portion of materialized data (out of a much larger dataset) a few times before investigating.

This behavior seems unexpected to me, given that data isn't actually loaded into memory. It may or may not conflict with goals of {vroom} (which I believe are focused more on clock-time than memory), but I didn't see it mentioned in another issue and thought it worth noting.

``` r
# Memory Usage with ALTREP columns ---------------------------------------------

# Install these if needed
# install.packages("lobstr")
# install.packages("vroom")
# install.packages("dplyr")
library(magrittr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
#> Warning: package 'magrittr' was built under R version 4.0.3

# Memory Usage Functions -------------------------------------------------------

# Note: I convert B -> MB using powers of 2 to match Windows

# R Memory in MB
r_mem <- function(digits = 2) {
  round(as.vector(lobstr::mem_used()) / 2^20, digits = digits)
}

# Combined R and System Memory in MB
mem <- function(quiet = FALSE) {
  gc()
  m <- c(R = r_mem(), Sys = memory.size())
  if (!quiet) print(m)
  m
}

# Object size in MB
o_size <- function(..., env = parent.frame(), quiet = FALSE) {
  gc()
  s <- round(as.vector(lobstr::obj_size(..., env = env)) / 2^20, digits = 2)
  if (!quiet) print(s)
  s
}

# Example ----------------------------------------------------------------------

# Task manager values were taken from a manual run just prior to the reprex

# Data will be 1,000,000 x 500 and saved to a temporary file
cols <- paste0("c", 1:500)
size <- 1e6L
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")

# Memory used: R vs System
m_init <- mem()
#>     R   Sys 
#> 37.04 52.92
# Task Manager: ~ 100.4 MB
m_init <- c(m_init, TM = 100.4)

# Create example data
data <- replicate(NROW(cols), sample(letters, size, TRUE)) %>%
  magrittr::set_colnames(cols) %>%
  dplyr::as_tibble()

# Object size
s_data <- o_size(data)
#> [1] 3814.76

# Memory used: R vs System
m_data <- mem()
#>       R     Sys 
#> 3856.83 3903.13
# Task Manager: ~ 3935.3 MB
m_data <- c(m_data, TM = 3935.3)

# Save data as CSV
vroom::vroom_write(data, tmp)

# Size of CSV file
round(file.size(tmp) / 2^20, digits = 2L)
#> [1] 953.68

# Remove in-memory data
remove(data)

# Memory used: R vs System
m_rm <- mem()
#>     R   Sys 
#> 44.15 61.39
# Task Manager: 121.4 MB
m_rm <- c(m_rm, TM = 121.4)

# Load data with `vroom()`
vdata <- vroom::vroom(
  tmp,
  col_types = vroom::cols(.default = vroom::col_character()),
  altrep = TRUE
)

# Object size
s_vdata <- o_size(vdata)
#> [1] 0.11

# Memory used: R vs System
m_vdata <- mem()
#>     R   Sys 
#> 45.44 61.76
# Task Manager: ~ 3936.3 MB
m_vdata <- c(m_vdata, TM = 3936.3)

# Delete data
remove(vdata)

# Memory used: R vs System
m_vrm <- mem()
#>     R   Sys 
#> 45.29 61.75
# Task Manager: ~ 120.7 MB
m_vrm <- c(m_vrm, TM = 120.7)

# Results ----------------------------------------------------------------------

# Original data size
s_data
#> [1] 3814.76

# Difference from added session memory
s_data - (m_data - m_init)
#>      R    Sys     TM 
#>  -5.03 -35.45 -20.14

# Difference from removed session memory
s_data - c(m_data - m_rm)
#>      R    Sys     TM 
#>   2.08 -26.98   0.86


# `vroom()` data size
s_vdata
#> [1] 0.11

# Difference from added session memory
s_vdata - (m_vdata - m_rm)
#>        R      Sys       TM 
#>    -1.18    -0.26 -3814.79

# Difference from removed session memory
s_vdata - (m_vdata - m_vrm)
#>        R      Sys       TM 
#>    -0.04     0.10 -3815.49
```

title: Parsing failure of CSV with lines ending with a space
description:
A follow-up of https://github.com/tidyverse/readr/issues/1207 (thanks for having looked at it) : it doesn't seem to work  either in vroom...

When a CSV file has a space character at the end of the line, outside a quoted value `vroom::vroom` can’t parse the file.

``` r
library(vroom)
#> Warning: le package 'vroom' a été compilé avec la version R 4.0.3
library(purrr)
library(stringr)

bad_csv <- tempfile()
```

A malformed CSV with one space character before newlines. A sample of 4 rows x 2 cols from a dataset found in the wild at <https://www.data.gouv.fr/fr/datasets/r/1913d0d6-d650-409d-a19e-b7c7f09e09a0> (caution : 180 MB)

``` r
writeLines('cddept,referenceprel
"047","04700069482" 
"047","04700069482" 
"047","04700069482" 
"047","04700069482" ', bad_csv)
```

`base::read.csv` can handle it and returns a 4x2 data.frame

``` r
read.csv(bad_csv) 
#>   cddept referenceprel
#> 1     47    4700069482
#> 2     47    4700069482
#> 3     47    4700069482
#> 4     47    4700069482
```

But `vroom::vroom` seems to ignore the newline and get lost

``` r
(df <- vroom::vroom(bad_csv))
#> Rows: 2
#> Columns: 2
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr [2]: cddept, referenceprel
#> 
#> Use `spec()` to retrieve the guessed column specification
#> Pass a specification to the `col_types` argument to quiet this message
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   cddept                referenceprel        
#>   <chr>                 <chr>                
#> 1 "047"                 "04700069482 \r\n047"
#> 2 "04700069482 \r\n047" "04700069482 \r\n047"
```

if we remove the space character at the end of every line…

``` r
nice_csv <- tempfile()
readLines(bad_csv) %>% 
  map_chr(~ str_replace(.x, "\\s$", "")) %>% 
  writeLines(nice_csv)
```

… `vroom::vroom` handles it fine and returns a data.frame 4x2

``` r
vroom::vroom(nice_csv)
#> Rows: 4
#> Columns: 2
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr [2]: cddept, referenceprel
#> 
#> Use `spec()` to retrieve the guessed column specification
#> Pass a specification to the `col_types` argument to quiet this message
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   cddept referenceprel
#>   <chr>  <chr>        
#> 1 047    04700069482  
#> 2 047    04700069482  
#> 3 047    04700069482  
#> 4 047    04700069482
```

title: Support UTF-16 encodings
description:
``` r
# This is the Byte Order Mark:
bom <- as.raw(c(255, 254))
# This is the text.
text <- "1\t2\n"

# Converted to UTF-16LE
text_utf16 <- iconv(text,from="UTF-8",to="UTF-16LE", toRaw = TRUE)[[1]]

# Write the BOM and the text to a file
tmp_file_name <- tempfile()
fd <- file(tmp_file_name, "wb")
writeBin(bom, fd)
writeBin(text_utf16, fd)
close(fd)

# read the file and use iconv to convert it to UTF-8
con <- file(tmp_file_name, "rb")
x <- readBin(con, "raw", n = 100)
vroom::vroom(iconv(list(x), from = "UTF-16LE", to = "UTF-8", toRaw = TRUE), col_names = FALSE)
#> Observations: 1
#> Variables: 2
#> dbl [2]: X1, X2
#> 
#> Call `spec()` for a copy-pastable column specification
#> Specify the column types with `col_types` to quiet this message
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>      X1    X2
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     2
```

<sup>Created on 2019-06-20 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

So we should basically be able to do this iconv conversion on the fly if given a multi-byte encoding.

title: `problems()` not interchangable between readr and vroom
description:
Not sure if this a bug _per se_ but it can be confusing when `vroom::problems()` masks `readr::problems()` and the two aren't interchangeable like `cols()`, etc.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(vroom) # masks readr

x <- "a,1\nb,2\nc"
dat1 <- vroom(x, delim = ",")
#> Rows: 2
#> Columns: 2
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr [1]: a
#> dbl [1]: 1
#> 
#> Use `spec()` to retrieve the guessed column specification
#> Pass a specification to the `col_types` argument to quiet this message
problems(dat1)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>     row   col expected  actual    file                            
#>   <int> <int> <chr>     <chr>     <chr>                           
#> 1     2     1 2 columns 1 columns /tmp/RtmpQ2jTrg/file7a7066e62b63
dat2 <- read_csv(x)
#> Warning: 1 parsing failure.
#> row col  expected    actual         file
#>   2  -- 2 columns 1 columns literal data
problems(dat2)
#> Error: Invalid input type, expected 'externalptr' actual 'list'
```

<sup>Created on 2021-02-09 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

I've been loading both readr and vroom in my scripts for a while and it took me a second to find the cause of this issue after upgrading vroom.

Maybe a more detailed error asking if the user used readr?

title: Issue with quotes?
description:
I'm trying to read the following CSV file, saved in `data.csv`:

```
id,title
633873,"Yanosik: ""antyradar"", korki, nawigacja, kamera"
```

I use the command: `vroom("data.csv", delim=",", escape_double=TRUE, quote="\"")`, with the latest version of `vroom`. The result:

```
# A tibble: 2 x 2
  id     title                   
  <chr>  <chr>                   
1 633873 "Yanosik: \"antyradar\""
2 korki  "nawigacja"    
```
Same result for `vroom("data.csv")`.

This seems incorrect. There should only be one row. When I use readr, everything works correctly: `read_csv("data.csv")`:

```
# A tibble: 1 x 2
      id title                                             
   <dbl> <chr>                                             
1 633873 "Yanosik: \"antyradar\", korki, nawigacja, kamera"
```

title: problems reading from .zip but not from decompressed file
description:
Hi, thank you for the excellent package! I am having some problems with expected != actual columns after reading a .csv file. I've narrowed it down to only experiencing the problems reading the original compressed .zip archive of the file, rather than the manually decompressed .csv file. 

```r
library(vroom)

# download zipped data
url <- "https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/files/2017/csv/2017_qtrly_singlefile.zip"
temp_dir <- tempdir()
data_zip <- tempfile(tmpdir = temp_dir, fileext = ".zip")
download.file(url, data_zip)

# decompress data
csv_basename <- unzip(data_zip, list=TRUE)$Name[1]
unzip(data_zip, files = csv_basename, exdir = temp_dir, overwrite=TRUE)
data_csv <- file.path(temp_dir, csv_basename)

# confirm problems with zip file only
vroom_from_zip <- vroom(data_zip)
problems(vroom_from_zip)
# A tibble: 1,058 x 5
     row   col expected   actual     file 
   <int> <int> <chr>      <chr>      <chr>
 1     2    33 42 columns 33 columns ""   
 2     2    33 42 columns 33 columns ""   
 3     2    33 42 columns 33 columns ""   
 4     2    33 42 columns 33 columns ""   
 5     2    33 42 columns 33 columns ""   
 6     2    33 42 columns 33 columns ""   
 7     2    33 42 columns 33 columns ""   
 8     2    33 42 columns 33 columns ""   
 9     2    33 42 columns 33 columns ""   
10     2    33 42 columns 33 columns ""   
# … with 1,048 more rows

vroom_from_csv <- vroom(data_csv)
problems(vroom_from_csv)
# A tibble: 0 x 5
# … with 5 variables: row <int>, col <int>, expected <chr>,
#   actual <chr>, file <chr>
```

Do you have any insights?

title: Specifying column types for optional columns
description:
I have some CSV files where some of the column are optional but I still want to specify the column type. I didn't find any good way of doing this with `vroom`.

For example the column `z` is optional

``` r
library(vroom)

vroom(
  I("x,y\n1,2\n3,4\n"),
  col_types = cols(
    x = col_double(),
    y = col_double(),
    z = col_double()
  )
)
#> Warning: The following named parsers don't match the column names: z
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     2
#> 2     3     4
```

<sup>Created on 2021-03-01 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

It basically works but I get a warning. Suppressing the warning doesn't seem like a good option to me as there might be other valid warnings. I cannot really use the `.default` argument as I have optional columns of different types.

I think `col_select` would be the easiest and most logical way how to specify these optional columns but it doesn't work as it is only applied after reading the data.

title: Duplicated factor levels for quoted characters
description:
Factor levels can get duplicated under certain circumstances

``` r
library(vroom)

vroom(
  I(r"{"day";"time"
"Sun";"Dinner"
"Sat";"Dinner"
"Sat";"Dinner"}"),
  col_types = list(
    day = col_factor(),
    time = col_character()
  ),
  delim = ";"
)$day
#> [1] Sun Sat Sat
#> Levels: Sun Sat Sat
#> Warning in print.factor(x): duplicated level [3] in factor

# first line removed -> works
vroom(
  I(r"{"day";"time"
"Sat";"Dinner"
"Sat";"Dinner"}"),
  col_types = list(
    day = col_factor(),
    time = col_character()
  ),
  delim = ";"
)$day
#> [1] Sat Sat
#> Levels: Sat

# not quoted -> works
vroom(
  I(r"{day;"time"
Sun;"Dinner"
Sat;"Dinner"
Sat;"Dinner"}"),
  col_types = list(
    day = col_factor(),
    time = col_character()
  ),
  delim = ";"
)$day
#> [1] Sun Sat Sat
#> Levels: Sun Sat
```

title: Cannot specify col_types for columns with missing names
description:
I have a relatively heavy `.csv` file (over 110MB) that I routinely analyze and use the `vroom()` for data import.  Recently, I decided to be explicit with the `col_types` parameter but vroom keeps throwing an error because one of the column names is missing. I noticed that this does not happen with the `readr::read_csv()` but it is significantly slower. Would be helpful to have this addressed also in `vroom`. Thank you.

```
library(vroom)
vroom("x,\n1,2\n3,4", delim = ",", col_types = cols(
    x = col_double(),
    `...2` = col_double()
))
#> New names:                                                                                                             
#> * NA -> ...2
#> Error: Invalid input type, expected 'list' actual 'NULL'
#> In addition: Warning message:
#> The following named parsers don't match the column names: ...2 

library(readr)
read_csv("x,\n1,2\n3,4", col_types = cols(
    x = col_double(),
    `X2` = col_double()
))

#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>     x    X2
#>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     2
#> 2     3     4
#> Warning message:
#> Missing column names filled in: 'X2' [2] 
```

title: `vroom` requires all columns in all files before checking `col_select`
description:
When getting data from my data sources, I often have to do it in chunks (old GUI software; we're working on it).  This often means I have to click through and select the variables I need multiple times. Sometimes I include an extra variable on one chunk/file but not another.  

When I import multiple files with `vroom`, it seems like I should be able to use `col_select` to select the columns I want. Even if some files have variables the others don't, as long as each file has all of the variables listed in `col_select` it seems like this should still work. 

Instead, this happens:

```
library(tidyverse)
library(vroom)

df1 = mtcars %>% select(mpg, cyl, disp, hp) %>% head()
df2 = mtcars %>% tail()

dir.create("test/")

vroom_write(df1, "test/df1.csv", delim = ",")
vroom_write(df2, "test/df2.csv", delim = ",")


files = list.files("test/", full.names = T)
combo = vroom(files, col_select = c("mpg", "cyl", "disp", "hp"))
```

With the error:
```
Error in vroom_(file, delim = delim %||% col_types$delim, col_names = col_names,  :                                                                                      
  Files must all have 4 columns:
* File 2 has 11 columns
```

Can `vroom` check to make sure all variables specified in `col_select` are present in each file instead of requiring all files to have the same number of variables? That way, the above example would return a data.frame with only `mpg`, `cyl`, `disp`, and `hp` in it?

title: Reading data with decimal mark ',' and col_type 'd' gives incorrect values
description:
Reading data that uses comma as the decimal separator and specifying double format doesn't work - the values read as NA. It reads correctly if specified as 'number' format.

``` r
library(vroom)

# Data using comma as the decimal mark
df = tibble::tribble(
  ~value,
  "23,4"
)

# Make a test data file
temp_path = tempfile()
vroom_write(df, temp_path)

# Reading with decimal mark ',' and col_type 'd' fails
df = vroom(temp_path, delim='\t',
           locale=locale(decimal_mark=','),
           col_types=cols('d'))

print(df)
#> Warning: One or more parsing issues, see `problems()` for details
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   value
#>   <dbl>
#> 1    NA

problems(df)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 5
#>     row   col expected actual file                                              
#>   <int> <int> <chr>    <chr>  <chr>                                             
#> 1     2     1 a double 23,4   C:/Users/kjohnson/AppData/Local/Temp/Rtmpi0fHjm/f~

# Reading with decimal mark ',' and col_type 'n' gives correct result
df = vroom(temp_path, delim='\t',
           locale=locale(decimal_mark=','),
           col_types=cols('n'))

print(df)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 1
#>   value
#>   <dbl>
#> 1  23.4

problems(df)
#> # A tibble: 0 x 5
#> # ... with 5 variables: row <int>, col <int>, expected <chr>, actual <chr>,

```

title: Incorrect row numbers, duplicate rows in `problems()` for `vroom_fwf`
description:
When parsing a fixed width file that contains invalid characters in supposedly numerical fields, I'm seeing incorrect line numbers in `problems()`. `problems()` also gains duplicated rows if I do more manipulations to the affected variables.

vroom wasn't reporting any problems at all until I performed an operation that required accessing the actual values. Is this expected as a consequence of vroom's lazy data access? (It presents some obvious challenges in a pipeline where `problems()` suddenly populates itself with a warning several steps away from the import)

When I encountered this in the wild with a >5000 row file, `problems()` was reporting unexpected values on rows: 144, 145, 156, 240, 244, 389, and 429. The actual problem rows in the file were: 1295, 1300, 1401, 2159, 2192, 3501, and 3860. (Needless to say, this was confusing!) The strange growth of `problems()` after performing additional operations involving the affected columns also occurred, with all the extra entries being assigned a row number of 1.

``` r
library(vroom)

fwf_text <- " 1  1\n .  . \n .  . "

layout <- list(
  start = c(1, 4),
  end   = c(2, 5),
  col_names = c("V1", "V2"),
  col_types = "ii"
)

fwf <- vroom_fwf(
  fwf_text,
  col_positions = fwf_positions(
    start = layout$start,
    end = layout$end,
    col_names = layout$col_names

  col_types = layout$col_types
)

problems(fwf)
```

title: Compressed file fails (uncompressed okay)
description:
Greetings. I've been having some trouble reading in a gz compressed table. Vroom messes up some of the lines, but works if I decompress it first. `read_csv()` works fine on the compressed table. 

I hope this is enough info to find the problem. The file is not huge (116 MB, 52,767 rows, 41 cols). 

Importantly, this issue is with vroom 1.4.0. I just tested in vroom 1.3.2, and that works without any problems.

Thanks!

Some code:

```r
# remote path
file.remote <- "https://github.com/genner-lab/meta-fish-lib/raw/main/assets/reference-library-master.csv.gz"

# try with read_csv - works
readr::read_csv(file.remote,guess_max=99999) %>% spec()

# try with vroom - col types are not as expected
vroom::vroom(file.remote,delim=",",guess_max=99999) %>% spec()
vroom::vroom(file.remote,delim=",",guess_max=99999) %>% problems()
```

If I download the file locally I get the same issue with the gz archive, but if I decompress it outside of R, vroom loads it correctly.

```sh
wget "https://github.com/genner-lab/meta-fish-lib/raw/main/assets/reference-library-master.csv.gz"
gzip -dk "~/reference-library-master.csv.gz"
```
```r
# local paths
file.local.gz <- "~/reference-library-master.csv.gz"
file.local.csv <- "~/reference-library-master.csv"

# vroom incorrectly loads the gz as before
vroom::vroom(file.local.gz,delim=",",guess_max=99999) %>% problems()

# vroom loads csv correctly now
vroom::vroom(file.local.csv,delim=",",guess_max=99999) %>% problems()
```

I tracked down the issue to a specific line (20964), but I can't see what is wrong with it.

```r
# works! 
vroom::vroom(file.local.gz,delim=",",guess_max=99999,n_max=20963) %>% problems() 

# does not work :(
vroom::vroom(file.local.gz,delim=",",guess_max=99999,n_max=20964) %>% problems() 
```

title: Reading directly to data.frames seems slower with version 1.4.0
description:
Hello,

@nealrichardson and I have been working on some benchmark tooling to help us benchmark our work in the Arrow project. In the process of that we've seen some performance changes in vroom that we were surprised by: with version 1.4.0 we're seeing a pretty large (3-4x) jump in total time to read some large files into a data.frame (i.e. with `altrep = FALSE`). We've tried a few different csvs to make sure it's not something specific in these files (happy to send along links to the files/more timings from them..

We've also tried separating these csvs by data type (i.e. pulling all of the character columns out of one and saving that as a separate csv and reading it in) to see if those have any impact and it looks like the problem is more pronounced for numeric and numeric-like types (integers, floats, and datetimes). The character-only csv was read in at similar speeds across the two versions (again, happy to send our code/timings for this as well).

Using the taxi data from January 2013 [from the vroom benchmarks](https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/blob/master/inst/bench/download-data.sh#L7):

title: Support comments within data
description:
Will need to change how the index works and include the beginning of the line in the index. This will add an additional index entry for each line of the file, but it cannot be helped if we want to support comments within data.

It may also make dealing with windows newlines a bit simpler, as we can break at the '\r' instead of at the '\n' + arithmetic.

title: Escape double = TRUE slower than readr and crashing.
description:
I have a 2.7GB dataset with "quirky" characters (e.g., "\T" in some description fields). When reading with readr (foo_1) with escape_double = F, from an S3 bucket I have a long waiting time but it is stable. When running the "same" function in vroom (foo_2), R hangs (taking up 10x times to read) and then crashes:

```
foo_1 <- function(x){
  readr::read_delim(x, "\t", escape_double = FALSE, locale = locale(), trim_ws = TRUE)
}

foo_2 <- function(x){
  vroom::vroom(x, delim = "\t", escape_double = FALSE, locale = locale(), trim_ws = TRUE)
}


# importing from S3 bucket (long time, but stable)
d <- aws.s3::s3read_using(foo_1, 
                           object = file, 
                           bucket = "my-bucket") 

# importing from S3 bucket (crashes after hanging)
d <- aws.s3::s3read_using(foo_2, 
                           object = file, 
                           bucket = "my-bucket") 
```


Is this a known bug?

title: incorrect docs in vroom_write?
description:

(As an aside, I'm consulting said docs to find out why on Windows, `vroom_write(data, filepath)` is failing with an error "cannot open file for writing", while the same code passes on Mac and Linux, and passes with base R's `write.csv`)

title: vroom::spec returns NULL when col_select is specified and readr is loaded
description:
When `readr` is loaded, calling `vroom::vroom` with a `col_select` argument returns a data frame without a `spec` attribute so `vroom::spec()` returns `NULL`.

``` r
library(vroom)

# This works
df <- vroom(vroom_example("mtcars.csv"), col_select=-mpg)
#> Rows: 32
#> Columns: 11
#> Delimiter: ","
#> chr [ 1]: model
#> dbl [10]: cyl, disp, hp, drat, wt, qsec, vs, am, gear, carb
#> 
#> Use `spec()` to retrieve the guessed column specification
#> Pass a specification to the `col_types` argument to quiet this message

vroom::spec(df)
#> cols(
#>   model = col_character(),
#>   mpg = col_skip(),
#>   cyl = col_double(),
#>   disp = col_double(),
#>   hp = col_double(),
#>   drat = col_double(),
#>   wt = col_double(),
#>   qsec = col_double(),
#>   vs = col_double(),
#>   am = col_double(),
#>   gear = col_double(),
#>   carb = col_double(),
#>   .delim = ","
#> )

library(readr)
#> Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'readr':
#>   method           from 
#>   format.col_spec  vroom
#>   print.col_spec   vroom
#>   print.collector  vroom
#>   print.date_names vroom
#>   print.locale     vroom
#>   str.col_spec     vroom
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'readr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:vroom':
#> 
#>     as.col_spec, col_character, col_date, col_datetime, col_double,
#>     col_factor, col_guess, col_integer, col_logical, col_number,
#>     col_skip, col_time, cols, cols_condense, cols_only, date_names,
#>     date_names_lang, date_names_langs, default_locale, fwf_cols,
#>     fwf_empty, fwf_positions, fwf_widths, locale, output_column,
#>     problems, spec

# This returns a data frame with no 'spec' attribute
df <- vroom(vroom_example("mtcars.csv"), col_select=-mpg)

vroom::spec(df)
#> NULL
```

title: vroom as a readr backend
description:
This issue is uses to track issues needed to use vroom as a readr backend.

- [x] Error reporting
- [x] Embedded newlines with multi-threads
- [x] Quoting behavior (#224)
- [ ] File handles
- [ ] On-disk indexes
- [x] NA handling

# Error reporting

We need a framework report shape (wrong number of columns) and parsing errors (wrong type of value) in similar format as readr. This is complicated because of multi-threading and lazy reading. A way to handle this is a class that locks updates with a mutex, and probably issue a warning when the first issue is found.

This is also complicated because often the code doesn't know the row, or the column, or the file it is reading. e.g. when indexing in parallel we don't know the row, because it depends on how many rows are in other threads. When reading values from altrep vectors we don't know the column, because the column type doesn't store what index it corresponds to.

# Embedded newlines

Currently to handle embedded newlines we say you need to disable multi-threading. This is unfortunately not robust enough, and we should instead do something similar to Ge, Chang and Li, Yinan and Eilebrecht, Eric and Chandramouli, Badrish and Kossmann, Donald, [Speculative Distributed CSV Data Parsing for Big Data Analytics](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/speculative-distributed-csv-data-parsing-for-big-data-analytics/), SIGMOD 2019.

A simple way to handle this would be to throw an error if you are using multiple threads and a newline is detected inside a quoted field, with the error message saying you need to re-parse with `num_threads = 1`. Or possibly we could even automatically re-parse ourselves when this occurs.

Alternatively we could employ the parallel 2 pass algorithm from the paper. It is slower than the speculative one, but simpler and easier to implement.

# Quoting behavior

Currently vroom uses a fairly naive way of handling and escaping quotes. It allows a quote to occur anywhere in a field, rather than only right before or after a delimiter. This unfortunately means with the default quote option if there is a field with only a _single_ unpaired quote the rest of the file is treated as quoted. We need to restrict this to only looking at quotes before or after a delimiter.

# On-disk indexes

The current index is always stored in memory, which can be prohibitive for very large files. Experiments using a mmapped file instead showed _faster_ index creation times with only minimal difference in value extraction time. This would also scale to arbitrarily big files (assuming you are only using part of the file). The major downside is you then also need to hold file handles for the indexes, which makes that problem worse. There is also a question of where the index should be stored, probably `tempdir()`, but what happens if there is not enough space there?

# File handles

Vroom currently holds an open file handle for every index. If we use the on-disk index each thread would have a separate file handle. So we would have `num_threads * num_files` potential open file handles. Ideally we would hold at max `num_threads` handles open at a time. One downside to not keeping open file handles is this ensures the files remain until all data is read from them. If we don't keep an open file handle the file could be deleted out from under us.

# NA handling

currently we only check for NA values for character and factor columns. Other column types do not explicitly check for the NA values. This wasn't a big deal until we gained better error reporting, but now these values will mistakenly show up in the problems dataset. This is somewhat trick to do, as we supply the NA values in the native encoding, the values are parsed as raw bytes, and we have to somehow detect the NA values without running re-encoding every value.

title: More robust handling of quoted fields
description: There are a number of issues where people run into problems by having quotes within their unquoted fields. Right now we unconditionally search for quotes anywhere in a field, we instead need to only treat a quote as a real one if it is not escaped _and_ occurs next to the delimiter. This is ultimately what readr does with these types of inputs and it seems to give more robust results in the real world.

title: Incorrect use of new.env function
description:
The following statement:
https://github.com/r-lib/vroom/blob/94fb48b4e9e471a17bd814e3f771967e695989ba/R/vroom.R#L270
relies on the wrong behavior of the `new.env` internal function in GNU-R, and produces a coerce error in FastR interpreter.
The signature is `new.env(hash = TRUE, parent = parent.frame(), size = 29L)`, therefore `emptyenv()` is bound to `hash`. Unfortunatelly, GNU-R behaves incorrectly (if you are interested in details, it is visible in `builtin.c` source in `do_newenv` function).

The correct version of the aforementioned statement is `cached <- new.env(parent=emptyenv())`.

title: Vroom issue with too many files (linux)
description:
When trying to read multiple files (10,000 files) in linux it raises a error saying that there are too many files open and then complains that one of the files doesn't have the same number of columns (which I am pretty sure it's not true). I already saw this issue #180 but the problem occurs in linux for my case while windows is fine. I don't have a Mac machine around so I couldn't check there.

```
mapping error: Too many open files
Error in vroom_(file, delim = delim %||% col_types$delim, col_names = col_names,  :
  Files must all have 2 columns:
* File 1018 has 0 columns
Calls: <Anonymous> -> vroom_
Execution halted
```

For what I know linux has a soft limit in the number of open files that can be checked with with `ulimit -Sn` (see [this](https://www.tecmint.com/increase-set-open-file-limits-in-linux/)). I did increase the limit to 12k files which should be sufficient to deal with the current problem and indeed it does workaround it. However I get another (unrelated?) issue. Not sure if this would be a valid workaround for me anyway because in some machines I don't have sudo so can be hard to change the system params.

```
Error: 'vec_as_names' is not an exported object from 'namespace:vctrs'
Execution halted
```

After updating the package `vctrs` it managed to run alight. I am not sure why it didn't update with vroom as this package is not loaded in the session info output of the linux devices but it does appear in the windows one. 

I set up a repo for reproducibility if useful. There are more details there that might be useful.

title: vroom causes progress::progress_bar to flicker (in some cases)
description:
Consider this example of iterating over vroom reading in a bunch of different files:

```r
setwd(tempdir())
library(vroom)

files <- paste0("dummy", 1:1880, ".csv")
x <- lapply(files, function(f) vroom_write(iris, f))
```


```r
pb <- progress::progress_bar$new(
  format = "  importing [:bar] :percent eta: :eta",
  total = length(files),
  clear = FALSE,
  width = 60,
  show_after = 0)


## progress bar FLICKERS off and on, unreadable
for(f in files){
  pb$tick()
  suppressMessages({
  df <- vroom(f)
  })
  
}
```

Compare to base R, no flickering:

```r
pb <- progress::progress_bar$new(
  format = "  importing [:bar] :percent eta: :eta",
  total = length(files),
  clear = FALSE,
  width = 60,
  show_after = 0)

for(f in files){
  pb$tick()
  suppressMessages({
    df <- read.csv(f)
  })
  
}
```

The issue seems to go away if I use a smaller number of files in the iteration.

title: Error "r_vector" when defining col_types with readr::cols()
false equivalence in vroom/tests/testthat/test-factor.R (due to utils::all.equal not testing factors well)
description:
Some of the tests in vroom/tests/testthat/test-factor.R pass in R and fail in TERR even though the objects created are identical in R and TERR.  I found that this was due to R's util::all.equal() not being strict enough when comparing factors.  Here is simplified version of one of the tests.

```r
t <- tibble::tibble(X1 = factor(c(NA, "b", "a"), levels = c("a", "b", NA), exclude = NULL))
v <- vroom::vroom("NA\nb\na\n", col_names = FALSE, col_types = list(X1 = col_factor(levels = c("a", "b", NA))), delim="\n")                                                                                                                      all.equal(t$X1, v$X1)
#R:  [1] TRUE
#TERR: [1] "missing value mismatches: 1"
```

R and TERR agree that there are no NAs in t$X1 and that the first element of v$X1 is an NA:

```r
> is.na(t$X1)
[1] FALSE FALSE FALSE
> is.na(v$X1)
[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE
They both produce the same t$X1 and v$X1:
> dput(t$X1)
structure(3:1, .Label = c("a", "b", NA), class = "factor")
> dput(v$X1)
structure(c(NA, 2L, 1L), .Label = c("a", "b", NA), class = "factor")
```

TERR's `all.equal(x,y)` for factors compares `is.na(x)` and `is.na(y)` and apparently R's does not (https://bugs.r-project.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=17897).   I think this difference in behavior between tibble and vroom is significant enough that it should be fixed.

title: View():ing an emptly tibble originating from vroom crashes Rstudio server session
description:
I'm running R-workloads on the open source rstudio-server with vroom and have encountered an issue with empty tibbles.

I'm not sure if this is an rstudio-issue, or a vroom issue, but seems to be pretty specific to vroom, so posting here.

The following code crashes the rserver-session every time:

```
aa <- data.frame(b = 1:3, c=letters[1:3])
write.csv(aa, "small_data.csv")
tt <- vroom::vroom("small_data.csv")
tt # Contents printed out nicely
View(tt) # Contents displayed ok

ttt <- tt[FALSE,]
ttt # Empty tibble printed out ok
View(ttt) # R crashes
```

This happens also if I use dplyr's filter to produce the empty tibble, but the above example aims to have minimal other dependencies.

My R-version is 3.6.2
rstudio-server is 1.2.5033 running on debian 10
vroom is at 1.2.1 (1.2.0 has the same issue) 


Note: an empty data.frame is displayed ok with View as is an empty tibble not produced by Vroom:
```
aa <- data.frame(b = 1:3, c=letters[1:3])
aaa <- aa[FALSE, ]
View(aaa) # this works

aa <- tibble::tibble(b = 1:3, c=letters[1:3])
aaa <- aa[FALSE, ]
View(aaa) # this also works
```

p.s. rstudio on a windows desktop does not crash. (rstudio desktop 1.2.5019, R 3.5.3, vroom 1.2.0)
